newsitem.title: INDIA: India power shortages seen hurting investment.
newsitem.headline: India power shortages seen hurting investment.

text.p: India said on Tuesday that its acute electricity shortage had reached a critical point, and was beginning to adversely affect investments ardently wooed under a free-market reform programme.

"The recurring power failures even in the capital city of Delhi this winter underline the critical nature of the power problem throughout the country," the government said in its annual Economic Survey for 1996/97 (April-March).

The survey, presented to parliament by Finance Minister P. Chidambaram, listed a number of negative results of power outages in India, which launched an economic reform programme in 1991 to integrate its economy with the world.

"Because of unavailable, uncertain or erratic supplies from the public grid, the economy is paying a heavy price in the form of foregone production, lost exports of goods and services, frustrated investment intentions," the survey said.

It added that "recourse to high-cost captive power generation, loss of international competitiveness and barriers to the spread of information technology...is redefining the terms of production, technical progress and international specialisation throughout the world."
India says it needs investments worth $79 billion to ease power shortages.

According to the survey, India could add only 14,799 megawatts in power generation capacity during the first four years of its Eighth Five-Year Plan (1992-97), which had envisaged an addition of 30,858 megawatts in the five years.
The government's survey identified several reasons for slippages in power generation.

The problems are linked to a paucity of funds, supply of equipment, land acquisition, territorial disputes, disturbed conditions at plant sites, fuel linkages, contract failures and rehabilitation of people at power plant sites, the survey said.

The government said it was working on a strategy to ease the power shortage, which included an encouragement to greater doses of private capital and the restructuring of inefficient state-run power distribution utilities.
